speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the feeling of those who have to take part in the budget debate at this stage is well expressed by the French writer: Tout est dit et l'on vien trop tard- everything has been said, and we were born too late. Our particular system has been described as " government by discussion " Well, I am sure that nobody will deny that we are applying the democratic principle to its fullest extent. Our friends opposite have said that the budget offered by my hon. friend the Acting Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) is a colourless instrument, a standpat budget;-they have certainly done it great honour by discussing it so vehemently and for such a long time. Of course, we knew it could not satisfy them-nothing could satisfy them coming from this government. Remembrance of the past and fear of the future are responsible for the discretion of my hon.

The Budget-Mr. Lapointe
friends opposite in their expression of satisfaction with any action of the party which sits to your right, Sir. Their criticism has been directed against the manner in which the financial statement had been prepared and presented, and more particularly concerning accounts of the Canadian National Railways. They have used very strong language regarding it. Indeed, my knowledge of English has been improved-or otherwise-by listening to this debate, and I have added a few energetic words to my vocabulary. My friend from Fort William and Rainy River (Mr. Manion) has excelled himself, and probably others, in this respect. He did it-if he will forgive me for saying so-with the characteristic zeal, and even furore, of a neophyte. I have always noticed that when circumstances, or perhaps error of judgment, pervert a man into a Tory, he always becomes a very bitter Tory, a very strong disciple of the faith. He has a troubled sense of guilt, and he feels the necessity of justifying himself by all available methods. I have seen it stated in the papers that came from home this morning that my hon. friend will pay a visit to my city of Quebec next Saturday. From here I extend to him a hearty welcome, and as I have already been invited to go to Fort William it is possible that I may pay a return visit to my hon. friend.

speechtext:
Yes, the government is
in power, and it is going to stay in power.
I was reading the other day a very clever French book written by Monsieur Barthou- Le Politique-in which members of parliament taking part in discussions were advised that it is very unwise and very dangerous to interrupt all the time. When we show my hon. friend and his associates that the method of bookkeeping followed by the Acting Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) was the one in practice when his predecessors presented budgets to the House, even during the time of the member for West York (Sir Henry Drayton) and of Sir Thomas White-well, they tell us that has nothing to do with it. In other words, they are prepared to sacrifice these two gentlemen or anyone else on the altar of political exigency. I commend, Sir, this method of bookkeeping not because it was the method followed by the hon. member for West York but because I think it is the right and fair method. I submit it is fair that all our railway accounts are to be kept separately from the ordinary accounts of the country both as regards the national debt and as regards the operation and the effect of the operation of the railways on the surplus or deficit in connection with our national finances as a whole. And I may say that this practice is followed elsewhere. I have in my hand an issue of the Wall Street Journal of Tuesday, April 21, of this year, in which the accounts of the state of Switzerland are given. There the ordinary debt and the debt of the railways are dealt with separately and given separately; indeed, the debt of the railway is higher than the ordinary debt of the federation. Then, in another account they give the federal railroad statement, the operating surplus, the net capital charges, and either the surplus or the deficit, as the case may be. This is not withholding information; I submit that it is giving full and complete and understandable information. But apart from that it is the only fair method, both to the railway and to the government. We are operating these railways under a system of public ownership and we are obliged to give that system a fair trial. The people of Canada desire that these railways shall be operated free from political or government interference, and it is our policy that this shall be done. Our main responsibility, I claim, is in the appointment of

The Budget-Mr. Lapointe
the head of ithe railway. This government takes full responsibility for the appointment of Sir Henry Thornton, and if that appointment is challenged we are ready to join the issue and take up the challenge before the people of Canada at any time. Of course, when the national railways become a paying proposition-it will not be before a long time, but it will be before my hon. friends come back to office-hon. gentlemen apposite will be the first to ask that the accounts be kept separately. But at present the adoption of that course does not synchronize, to use a familiar term of days gone by, with their present policy of alarm, blue ruin, and panic.
My hon. friends emphasize in every possible way the unavoidable deficits for which they themselves are largely responsible. They magnify the importance of the deficits-and it is a strange way of giving public ownership a fair trial-but they never mention the fact that two years ago the Canadian National Railways had an operating surplus of $20,000,000 and that even last year they had an operating surplus of $17,000,000. What the railways are suffering from is the legacy of debt which has been left to the present administrators, but to refer to this also would not harmonize with the policy of preaching blue ruin and disaster so zealously followed by my hon. friends.
In speaking on the address the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen) complained that I had described him as a Jeremiah, and stated that he would not be deterred from stating the facts as they were. Well, I will never find fault with my right hon. friend or with anybody else for stating the facts as they are. But I protest against misrepresenting Canada in the face of the world. I protest against the demoralizing influence of a campaign which has the effect of supplying erroneous information and mischievous and misleading material to those who are carrying on anti-Canadian propaganda in Europe or elsewhere. Ind&ed, we read in the press that the agents of the government of Canada, both for immigration and trade, are complaining of the effect of that campaign. To say, for instance, that our manufacturers are closing down their plants and failing by the thousands is a statement which I claim should not be made by any public man in this country, unless it be true. If it is not true, it is not fair to the people of Canada and to the Canadian nation. Now, were failures so numerous in this country last year? I have in my hand a compilation of statistics made by Bradstreet's which appeared in the Financial Times, of
Montreal, of February 13, 1925. as to financial affairs in Canada during the year 1924. It shows that the failures in Canada in 1924 numbered 2.312, a decrease of 21.9 per cent from 1923, and of 28.8 per cent from 1922. But what is more interesting in this statement is that this agency of Bradstreet's gives the causes of those failures and statistics as to those causes, and what do we find with regard to those failures in Canada? I claim the liberty of giving this to Hansard.
Mr. Speaker, we are hearing much also about debt and taxes. Canada has been described on all the platforms of the country as being the country where we are most heavily burdened with debt, and where we are taxed much higher than any other country not only in the British Empire, but some have even said in the whole world. You will remember, Mr. Speaker, that last year I caused almost a commotion by stating in this House that Canada was the least taxed country in the British Empire. I was taken to task for having made such a statement, and the Ottawa Journal had an editorial in that connection deploring in gloomy terms the impropriety of a public man being guid.y of such grossly erroneous and false statements. Of course, it meant the falling down of the citadel of misrepresentations that had been erected in the preceding months.
This year I have asked the Bureau of Statistics to make the necessary researches into debt and taxation and prepare a statement to that effect, and I will ask you, Mr. Speaker,

The Budget-Mr. Lapointe
to permit Hansard to print their statement. What do I find there? It is that Canada has the least debt of all the countries of the empire, though larger than that of the United States, the latter being due to the fact that in Canada we own public utilities and railways and their debts are added to the national debt. The debt of Canada per capita is $442.46, and that includes federal debt, provincial debt and municipal debt. The debt of the United States, including all the debts of the states and all municipal debts, amounts to $268.57 per capita; Great Britain, $922.48; the Commonwealth of Australia, $820.58; New Zealand, $884.94; Union of South Africa, $647.52.
When it comes to taxation, the taxation per capita of Canada is $63.51, including taxes federal, provincial, municipal and school; United States, $68.49, or $5 more than in Canada; United Kingdom, $99.36; Australia. $69.22; New Zealand, $77.12; South Africa' $75.92. All the particulars as to the national debt, the provincial debt, and the municipal debt are given in detail in this statement, and I think it is important on account of the lack of knowledge as to this question to put this statement on Hansard1:

Of course, nobody likes to pay taxes, and it is a catchy appeal to refer to high taxation. I was reading some time ago the words of
an eminent English writer, who says that that man is highly educated who pays his taxes gladly. I am afraid that if we were to adopt this test as to education, few of us would qualify.
As regards the banks, I have statistics of all the deposits, but I do not think it is necessary to put those figures on Hansard.
Some gentlemen like to make comparisons with the United States. Well, Sir, first, it is not a fair comparison to make, because Canada was in the war from the very first day; it was not so with the United States. But even disregarding that, I think we stand the comparison pretty well. Three years ago our dollar was worth seventeen cents less than the American dollar; to-day it is just as valuable as the American dollar. The exports of the United States have increased to-day over what they were in pre-war times by 22 per cent; the exports of Canada have increased over what they were in pre-war times by 57 per cent.
Yes, Mr. Speaker, these are difficult times. The waters are stormy, and the strongest vessel has to struggle desperately to keep afloat, but our national ship is going along steadily and safely through the crisis which has disturbed and upset the world. The prophets of disaster may continue to stab themselves and cry out after the manner of an ancient pagan priest, but the economic process will go on its way in Canada towards a condition in which the means of well living will exist for all Canadians. We do not ask the leader of the opposition and hon. gentlemen opposite to help us, it is beyond their virtue, but at least will they not refrain from hindering, hampering and blocking the way? Through you, Mr. Speaker, I say to them "Play the game. Do not push your country back. Keep cheerful, or at least keep still". A very able French public man, whose name has again become prominent recently, was convicted and sentenced to deportation during the war because he was a defeatist-what the French call a defeatist. He was preaching despondency and representing that disaster was looming ahead of the French army. In war time, of course, this is a crime. In these times when all the problems of national and international life are coming together for solution, when the nations are still reeling under disturbances which have been unparalleled in history, defeatism although not a crime is at least a most unfair and unpatriotic system of dealing with one's country.
Now, with regard to the budget they describe it as a standpat budget, and the very

The Budget-Mr. Lapointe
same gentlemen who denounce it as being such are declaring vigorously that we must have stability in tariff matters. What do those worshippers of stability mean? Is not stability standpatism under another name? Does their conception of stability mean only non-interference with the budget when it is a question of lowering the duties, but when it is a question of increasing them then it is still stability? I cannot see any logic or consistency in such a contention. Under freedom only can real stability exist; and those gentlemen are the last in the world to desire freedom in trade matters. A protective tariff is essentially unstable. We hear very often the example of Prance given to us in that regard, especially by my hon friend for West York (Sir Henry Drayton). France is a high-protection country. Do you think that she has stability in tariff? In France-and I took the figures from a French financial review a few days ago-the tariff of 1892, which was described as possessing stability, was modified1 348 times between 1892 and 1908, and the tariff was changed in toto in 1910. From 1916 to January 1, 1923. sixty-five changes have afforded 3,294 modifications in the tariff. Well, I do not think that any serious minded man can claim that this is stability in tariff matters.
What about the amendment proposed by the hon. member for West York? Well, there has been a change of attitude. I remember well our first year after the general election when my hon. friend (Sir Henry Drayton) moved an amendment taking this government to task for not having fulfilled its pledges by reducing the tariff. He did not want, ol course, that the tariff should be decreased; on the other hand he was not satisfied with the government for not decreasing It. We were the subject of criticism in any event "You shall and you shan't, you will and you won't, ymu will be cursed if you do and you will be cursed if you don't." Then the word "protection" was in every amendment since, but this year it is sweetly eliminated from it. I read the other day that the style adopted in recent years by young ladies of bobbing their hair was going out of fashion. Apparently my hon. friend from West York was not aware of it. His amendment is outrageously bobbed; it is an emasculated political instrument deprived ,of all virility. My bon. friend from Chambly and Vercheres (Mr. Archambault) said the other day that it was an agglomeration of commonplace platitudes, and I agree with him. I am afraid that my hon. friend next year will move that in the opinion of the House babies are not brought [Mr. Lapointe, 1
into the world by storks. But if the amendment has not been very illuminating the debate has been illuminating in at least one respect. The very opposite lines of attack against our policy, coming as they do from extreme opposite angles, is the best illustration of the necessity of a middle course, of a policy of compromise trying to harmonize to the largest possible extent the apparently uncompromising attitude of my hon. friends _ opposite. Indeed the speeches of my hon. friends in one comer of the House are very well answered by the speeches of my bon. friends in the other corner and the first speeches were a reply in advance to those of my bon. friends angularly opposite. The intention to vote against the budget by gentlemen in this House, as expressed in their speeches is for wholly different and contradictory reasons, the one setting forth the extraordinary contention that a country whose territory is as large as the territory of Europe, and which has only nine millions of population spread over that expanse of country, rich in natural resources and wealth of all kinds, may enr'ch itself by erecting a wall around its boundaries and refusing financial and economic communication with the rest of the world; the other-and I will give my hon. friends of the Progressive party credit for greater sincerity of purpose than I do the official opposition-claiming that an industrial system which has been in force for a large number of years should be subject to a radical and immediate evolution or revolution at a time when normalcy has not yet resumed her position again in the world, and when conditions are most unfavourable to giving changes a fair chance of proving effective and beneficial. Such a conjunction of opposite forces is of a negative and destructive character. If successful it would merely prevent the government from functioning normally and would transform parliament into a crystallized deadlock. It is not a part of our public economy that it should be subject to any party which can paralyse but cannot replace it.
These divergent views show also very strikingly that circumstances and conditions of geography play a large part in determining the fiscal views of communities and individuals. Indeed, only yesterday a gentleman well known in this country, who was Minister of Public Works in the late administration, stated in the city of Toronto that he did not believe any longer in protection, not because of the unsoundness of the doctrine-he did not express any view on that-but because protection was no good for the province of

The Budget-Mr. Lapointe
Nova Scotia. We have a huge country, and we have sectional interests which are not identical and in many cases are widely different. Those who are entrusted with public functions are trustees, not for one class, not for one section of the community, but for the whole people and country of Canada. It is their duty to try to find out the causes of these divergences of interest, and to find if possible the concessions which it may be possible and desirable to obtain. Tariff stability may have its virtue, but national stability is preferable. The decision to be reached may sometimes be a choice of the second best, but then through all history politics have been in the main the acceptance of the second best against the impossible or the ideal. Newspaper editors, professors, or extreme partisans, may be displeased, but the practical man knows that his duty is to deal with practical affairs and not with theories of panic and despair. We need compromise and men of compromise.
Compromise in the sense of avoiding extremes is a truly characteristic British policy. It has made the empire and keeps it together. It is hated by ail extremists, either radical or reactionary. I tell you, in all sincerity, Mr. Speaker, the political party of Canada which will inscribe the word "Moderation" on its banner will stand amidst all others, like the rock of Gibraltar. It will be very dangerous and even destructive for this country-and I think everybody will agree with me on that statement-if extreme views on one side were to be followed in the direction of affairs by extreme views on the other side; in that case we would have to stand a succession of economic revolutions and counter-revolutions in this country. Open-mindedness and a recognition of t'he law of change is part of the Liberal doctrine, and with a reconsideration of policy when required we shall always be ready to face the situation: policies are made for men and not men for policies. May I say to my friends of the Progressive party that I think we have shown where we stand. We have reduced the tariff and have been violently attacked for it. Is it not desirable from the point of view of the advocates of low tariff to let our policy vindicate itself and to show that the high protectionists are wrong when they claim that the loss or decrease of revenue is due to the reduction of the tariff? Surely it is well to give the low tariff a fair trial. Moreover, people should not forget that it is an important and specific phase of our national policy. It is after all one of many thousand other factors that affect our social and national life. The physician diagnoses the disturbance of a single organ and treats it as a correlative part of the whole body. What physicians do
governments must do, and I think it is the only successful way.
Another subject about which I w?ish to say a word is the British preference. It is extraordinary to see the numerous misconceptions and the erroneous notions which exist with regard to this. Why, only recently it was stated in my own city that Sir Wilfrid Laurier had opposed the British preference. No more erroneous statement, of course, can be made. Sir Wilfrid Laurier was the father of the British preference. He pursued that policy to the end of hik life, and in the last speech he made before the Eastern Ontario Liberal Association he claimed that that policy had been back of the Liberal party, and he was proud to be able to say that he had been the originator of it. There are some who think it is a sentimental device in the interests of Great Britain and not in the interests of Canada. I do not hesitate to say-and everyone may take down my words-that if such were the case I would be opposed to the British preference. But the British preference has been conceived and carried out in the interests of Canada and Canadians; it is part of the low tariff policy of the Liberal party. The United States have erected a wall against the products of our farms and other products, and we have to find outlets for our trade. Was it not good policy to build up a trade with Great Britain, where our own goods go free? Was it not in the interests of Canada to build up a trade between the Mother Country and ourselves? Have we been the loser by reason of such policy? What has been the result? The very year after a preference was granted, in 189S, our exports to Great Britain increased from 875,000.000 to $100,000,000, and the progression has consistently continued until last year our exports amounted to $361,160,802. At the same time, last year, our imports from Great Britain were more than $153,000000, a good deal less than half the value ol our exports. Are we the losers? We so'it Great Britain that S361,000,000 worth of goods without paying one cent in duty. Great Britain has paid us over $28,000,000 in duty on the $150,000,000 of goods whicii she sold us. Are we the losers? Thirty-five per cent of our exports go to England while we receive from her only seventeen per cent of our imports. I repeat, are we the losers? Our goods are going to England free. Their goods are paying duty when sent to this country.

Our natural market is the United States, but we have difficulty of access to it. The United States made us an offer 4 p.m. of reciprocity in 1911. We cannot complain because we slammed the door back in the face of the Americans in that year; but we are facing conditions as they are, and we must find other markets. The British preference was one means of finding such a market, and commercial treaties with foreign countries are another means.
I am sorry that I do not see the familiar and friendly features of my hon. friend from Lincoln (Mr. Chaplin) as I want to say a word or two about the French treaty. Since that treaty was signed in 1922 it has got on his nerves and disturbed his sleep, and I am afraid I have to bear some of the responsibility for shortening the days of the hon. member. Last year he made a strong criticism of the treaty. There is no nicer gentleman in the world than my hon. friend' when we meet him privately, but last session I had to point out how unfair he was in criticizing the French treaty, and this session he has made the same mistake. He gives us a list of

The Budget-Mr. Lapointe

articles coming to this country, regarding which he says: They have paid such and such an amount of duty; if there had been no treaty negotiated in 1022 they would have paid a larger amount of duty; consequently the country has lost hundreds of thousands of dollars. Well, in 1922, when this treaty was signed, the general tariff was not applied by Canada to the products of France; but my friend is always basing his calculations on the general tariff. As a matter of fact, there had been a treaty in force since 1908. After the war France notified all nations with which she had treaties that those treaties were terminated. For some time there was no trade agreement between France and Canada, blit in 1921 the Minister of Trade and Commerce of the then government, Sir George Foster, entered into another trade agreement with France, which was ratified by this parliament, and under which Canada was applying to all products coming from France the most favourable tariffs that are or may be granted by Canada to the products of any third power except those of the United Kingdom or of the British dominions and possessions. To show what really w'ould happen, I have asked the officers of the Tariff branch of the Finance department to give me a couple of typical items, and they have selected silks and velvets. According to my hon. friend from Lincoln, the country would lose $169,000 on those two items alone. Why, if you base your calculation on the tariff as it was under the agreement entered into by my friends opposite, which was in force in 1922, and was then replaced by the present treaty, instead of losing $169,000 of duties, you will find we have increased our revenue by $30,000. This shows how unfair such a criticism is, and I do not think it should be indulged in.
Now, it may be asked, why was this treaty negotiated and signed when there was that trade agreement in existence. I answer, that it was because the Canadian manufacturers, as represented by the Canadian Manufacturers' Association, were complaining that under that agreement Canadian goods could not enter France on the same basis and under the same conditions as American goods. The treaty was negotiated at the instance of the manufacturers of Canada to give them on French territory the same rights and privileges as those enjoyed by the manufacturers of the United States, and I myself heard representatives of our agricultural implement industry congratulate and thank the government for having given them the privileges which they now enjoy under this treaty.

There is another criticism by my hon. friend, but for which I cannot blame him, because he based his figures on statistics given by the Department of Customs. He said that last year the balance of trade with France was against us by $5,000,000 or $3,000,000,- I do not remember which. As a matter of fact that is how it appears in the reports issued by the Customs department; but I was surprised to see that the reports as given by the French government for 1924 differ substantially from ours. This will be found in the Commercial Intelligence Journal of April 4:
The statistics of the French Department of Customs show that during 1924 the commercial relations between Canada and France can be viewed with considerable satisfaction. The value of merchandise exported to Canada almost doubled in 1924 as compared with 1923 -333,260,000 francs against 183,457,000 francs. The exports from Canada to France show a total increase of 109,130,000 francs-482,826,000 francs in 1924 against 373,000,000 odd in 1923.
So our exports are still much larger than our imports according to the figures issued by the French government; and surely everybody will admit that France would not show a balance of trade unfavourable to her if she could help it.

Now, I hasten to conclude my remarks. In commercial and economic as well as other matters our policy is dictated exclusively by the interests of Canada. Conditions are not what they were in 1878, when the so-called National Policy was launched. There was no west at that time. We have now four different and separate sections, and the true Canadian policy must consider all the interests and divergences of interest of all those sections. We cannot compare our conditions with those of homogeneous countries which are small in territory and uniform in interest; still less can we compare our situation with that of the United States, which though a protectionist country to all outside appearances, is really enjoying free trade among various states having an aggregate population of over 110,000,000. Arguments with regard to the home market which may be valuable there are preposterous in Canada; and to call "national" a policy which has the effect of selling Canadian goods cheaper to the inhabitants of the 166i
antipodes than to our own citizens is not sensible, in my judgment. The true national policy is one that will permit all Canadians to five and will give equal justice to all. That equal justice, I am afraid, cannot come from those who want everything their own way without considering the interests of others. It cannot come from any party which is eastern or western in its character and which policy appeals only to one or the other of our great geographical sections. How many times did we hear the suggestion made by different people in eastern Canada that Quebec and Ontario should unite against the activities of the west? I believe in Canada, in the whole of Canada, Canada for Canadians is a splendid policy, but it must be Canada for all Canadians, not for any privileged section of the people.
Mr. R. V. LeSUEUR (West Lambton): Mr. Speaker, I believe I should first relieve the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) of an apprehension which is apparently worrying him by stating at once that I am not a pessimist and that I have no desire to spread blue ruin. I believe that statement may be applied with equal force to all other hon. members sitting in this section of the House. In fact, I can assure the hon. Minister of Justice that we are essentially optimistic here and that our optimism grows every day as the election approaches.
I can say this also, Mr. Speaker: that being optimistic I would be just as happy as the Acting Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) could possibly be if conditions in Canada to-day permitted the people to practically forget the budget. But unfortunately that is not the case and the budget to-day remains the most important, the most eagerly awaited, and the most carefully studied pronouncement that the government makes during the session. For the same reason the office of Minister of Finance remains of an importance fully equal to that of the office of Prime Minister. I have no desire to detract from the prestige of that office, but frankly I get no satisfaction from the conditions which contribute so largely to that importance. I refer to the difficult financial situation and to the difficult financial problems which to-day face this country and to the prolonged continuance of the depression or readjustment, whichever you like to call it, which this country has been undergoing for the last four years, a
The Budget-Mr. LeSueur

depression or readjustment which is accentuated by the burden of still unreduced war time taxes. Sometimes, Sir, I fear that we have but a vague and hazy realization of our position. I believe the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) fully appraised the situation and that it fairly bewildered him. I believe that the ever-present weight of the problems connected with that situation contributed in no small degree to his ill-health, and for the sacrifice he made in that respect this Dominion owes him a great obligation.
I would like first to glance briefly at our trade conditions; and I may add that I do so partly on account of the divergence of opinion which exists in that regard, and partly in order to serve as a basis for my later remarks. The remarks of the Minister of Justice amply illustrate the divergence which prevails on this question. I shall endeavour to get a reasonably accurate view of it and to base my conclusion, so far as that is possible, on fundamental facts which must be admitted; then I shall see if we cannot arrive at som? remedies which will apply to our present difficulties.
First, we should keep in mind the fact that the last years of the war and the year or so thereafter produced a period of industrial expansion and considerable inflation. Immediately following that we had a period of depression which spread like a great pall over the whole civilized world. That period was marked by a recession in wages and in the standard of living which varied greatly in degree in the various countries affected. It was also marked by a rapid and uneven depreciation in currency and bjr a wild and uneven fluctuation in exchange. In view of these chaotic and highly irregular conditions in the various trading countries certain nations immediately took aggressive steps to protect their nationals. I want to deal briefly with this phase of the subject by way of following up to some extent what I said last year. France, we know, immediately increased her tariff to the highest point in her history. France has since that time been blessed with an expanding prosperity, her basic industries showing 'a marked increase and reaching today perhaps the highest point in her history. Her internal and external trade alike are at a pinnacle at the present time, and unemployment is unknown. I know some hon. member will have in mind the fact of the supposed recent financial difficulty in France. But I may explain that that was a proposal to increase the arbitrary limit which had been set to the note issue of the Bank of France from 41 milliards to 45 milliards. That in-

crease, however, was purely a financial measure to give further elasticity to their currency and enable it to meet the expanding demands of trade. That is the view taken in financial circles, I may say, and is fully explained in a very recent number of the London Statist.
The United States likewise took drastic and immediate measures in the depression of 1921 to protect her internal industrial life against what I have described as the chaotic and highly irregular trade conditions existing in other countries She had a most remarkable recovery and enjoyed ever increasing prosperity from about the first part of 1922 to possibly the end of the first quarter in 1924. At that time hter trade had a recession, but since September, 1924, and especially since she was reassured of a continuance of her strong and stable fiscal policy on November 4, 1924, the United States has recovered remarkably from the recession which she experienced in the second and third quarters of that year. The last number, the April issue, of the Federal Reserve Bulletin is clear evidence of that. It shows clearly that her production in basic industries is materially greater in January of 1925 than it was in January of 1924, and is materially higher than it was in the low quarters of 1924. Likewise her production in minerals, her manufacturing production and her agricultural movements are all greater. If we turn to her bank statements we find that the current loans for this January are much in excess of the current loans of the year before. Her bank debits are likewise higher, and her time deposits have correspondingly decreased, showing an increased activity in trade. I believe that is one of the best criterions. When you have larger current loans and smaller time deposits you know that the money is in circulation, being used in business, and that you have then greater business activity. I could take up other points in the United States, but I will point my remarks as to their prosperous condition by the statement of Andrew W. Mellon, that wizard of finance to whom the United States is so much obligated, and whose statements are generally regarded as those of a business man and not of a politician. He prophesies a continuance of good conditions in the United States, and says that present, conditions are fundamentally sound.
Now if we look at conditions as they exist in Canada to-day, we realize that Canada suffered from the same depression in 1921, and that such depression continued with more or less unvarying monotony during the years 1922 and 1923; that in the early part of 1924 there

The Budget-Mr. LeSveur
were signs of a recovery from our depression, but 1924 unfortunately did not fulfil those hopes, and we had through the greater part of 1924 an even worse trade condition than we had previously. Now I am glad to say that the early months of this year have shown signs of improvement. We have improved from the low point of 1924, so far as I can judge, but I doubt very much if we have yet come to the point where we were in the first quarter of 1924. In judging of that con-, dition, let us look first at our bank statements. We find that the current loans in our banks declined from an average of $938,000,000 in December to an average of about $908,000,000 in February. We must allow for seasonal fluctuation, because December represents possibly our busiest retail trade. But we find that February of this year is about $80,000,000 less than February of last year. If we take our bank debits, almost the same condition prevails. In March our bank debits show a slight improvement over March of last year, but the general result of the quarter is lower than the first quarter of last year. I might say that our time deposits, corresponding to what we find in our loans and debits, show an increase in the first three months of this year, showing that our people are putting their money in the banks on a time basis and business is quiet. Our time deposits again are greater than they were in the first quarter of last year. So it all goes to show that business activity, while it is possibly improving at the present time, is still considerably below what it was in the first quarter of 1924, which was-a period of depression^ I might also take up the question of our basic industries. In our basic industries production is also showing signs of improvement, especially in March, but allowing for seasonal fluctuation the general conclusion must be very nearly the same as is to be drawn from our bank statements, namely, that while we are showing signs of improvement we are still below our condition of 1924. I might take up the question of employment and find out just how we stand there. Taking January, 1920, as our index we find that our employment on March 1, 1923, was 89.9 per cent; on March 1, 1924, 90.7 per cent, and on March 1, of this year, 87 per cent, or about 3 per cent lower than for the corresponding period in either of the years 1923 or 1924. In this regard I might refer to some of the detailed statements which were placed on Hansard referring to specific industries by the hon. Minister of Labour (Mr. Murdock). I note, for instance, that he speaks of the employment in some 47 mills engaged in the manufacture
of woollen yarn and cloth. This table shows that the numbers employed in 1925, while gradually increasing, are less than the numbers employed in the same months in each of the years 1922, 1923 and 1924, exactly proving What I have stated. If we turn to his figures with regard to the boot and shoe industry, in which he takes 91 manufacturers as his test, we find exactly the same thing, that the employment in 1925, while improving, is still below the numbers employed in the years 1922, 1923 and 1924. I may add that I do not think any of the tables presented by the hon. Minister of Labour in his address to this House contradict or even reflect on the conclusion to which I have come. If he were here, I would ask him to point out any that did conflict, because I have gone carefully through them and I believe they are all in accord.
Before I leave the remarks of the Minister of Labour, I would like to point out one thing, and that is that he gives two tables with regard to the boot and shoe industry, one on page 2002 of Hansard, in which he sets forth for 1923, 189 establishments, with 12.439 wage earners, and a product value of practically $45,000,000, and then on the next page, for the same industry and the same year he sets forth the number of establishments as 121, the number of employees 10,903, and the value of production $36,000,000 odd Now, without adequate explanation these two tables are certainly most confusing, and in the minister's statement there is no explanation. Both tables are under the same headings and are for the same years, and show diametrically opposed figures. The~minisfer must either explaiiTthat, oN we can only conclude that he has disproved in the latter part of his speech what he attempted to prove in the earlier part.
Now, I believe that the more or less fundamental facts which I have given form a sufficient basis for the conclusion at which I have arrived, namely, that our condition is gradually improving and has improved from the low point of 1924, but that we are still suffering from a marked depression, and that that depression is as yet below what it was in the first quarter of 1924. Furthermore we have no clear and definite signs as to when this period of readjustment will end. or that we are going to continue improving and come back to normalcy.
Before leaving the subject of trade conditions I should like to indicate two conclusions which to my mind are Obvious. The first is that the actual results and facts have shown that France and the United States were wise in their action in protecting their internal industries against outside chaotic conditions.
The Budget-Mr. LeSucur

By reason of that protection France has enjoyed tremendous prosperity and could to-day, I believe, without serious injury to her nationals increase her taxation. The United States has likewise prospered largely by reason of adopting the same measures, and has been enabled, largely on that account, to decrease her taxation and reduce her war debt. The second conclusion which appears to me obvious is this:	It is inconceivable, at least
to me, how in the face of our present trade depression, and with no clear and definite signs of a recovery from that depression, we can ciaim that we are enjoying great prosperity. I am firmly persuaded that a stable fiscal policy, administered with the advice of a competent tariff board, is a primary factor in the recovery of our country. I would further say that we should not endeavour to spread a measure of optimism among our people by unduly optimistic statements. The better way to proceed would be to inaugurate a campaign of intensive economy as to which I shall have some suggestions to offer, and a rigid reduction of expenditures, apart altogether from political considerations.	One of the
greatest grounds for confidence and one of the greatest factors in inspiring confidence is when a business in times of stress cuts its expenditure to the bone even to the smallest items. Such a course inspires confidence among the people connected with that industry, and not indulgence in unduly optimistic talk.

Since the year 1924 we have advanced a smaller proportion of the requirements of the National railway system in cash, and a greater proportion by way of bonds guaranteed by the Dominion. In the year 1925 our railways required 82 millions and some odd thousand dollars. The balance of $64,000,000 or thereabouts, was raised by bonds guaranteed by the Dominion and then handed over to the railway system and appears as an indirect obligation. The substance was the same; only the form was different. Therefore, all that I will say about immigration is this: I believe that owing to the essentially individualistic and economic character of migratory movements to-day and owing to the conditions in certain countries of Europe and to the regulations as to emigration to the United States, we have to-day an exceptionally good opportunity for an aggressive immigration policy. The essential need in a real immigration policy appears to be co-operation between the Dominion government, the various provincial governments, and the Empire Settlement Board. The next point is that owing to the nature of immigration you have got to have an inducement for the immigrant; I believe the greatest inducement which we can offer is that the immigrant will be taken care of when he locates in this country, and if that inducement is to be solid, it must be on a more or less sound and businesslike foundation. Now let me say in conclusion that I have endeavoured this afternoon to present a reasonably accurate view of our trade conditions and the necessity of reducing our taxes in an endeavour to better that position; also to give a fairly accurate view of our financial situation and the way we are heading. I have suggested some remedies. These remedies I may briefly summarize as follows: First, I believe that we must have a strong and stable fiscal policy, administered as I have said with the advice of a competent tariff commission Which will reasonably assure our industries of intelligent, stable and businesslike treatment. Second, that we should have an aggressive attack on our expenditures in the routine business of government that we should deal with our expenditures in the same way as any business corporation would, and should establish inter-departmental boards with the object of bringing up-to-date modem business methods into our routine business and by co-operation and team work, eliminate waste and duplication. Third, I believe that we should establish a check or governor on the expenditures of our railway system. And lastly, which is possibly the kernel of the whole business, I think that our government should stop the policy of drifting along in apparent helplessness without facing squarely the difficulties which confront them; and their slogan should be "Business and results," not "politics."

subtopic: STATEMENT OF DEBT AND TAXATION OF ENGLISH-SPEAKING COUNTRIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker. I have listened with much pleasure to the address which has just been delivered. It stands out very brilliantly in comparison with much of the partisan debate that we have heard so far. I will try to follow the ideal set by the hon. gentleman and in doing so will endeavour to speak without prejudice, actuated by the sole desire to examine the question "What is wrong with Canada?" and if possible suggest an answer.
Canada is so diversified in its interests and outlook that no solution can be arrived at unless a spirit of sympathy and genuine cooperation holds sway. Lacking such co-operation between the different units that make up the Canadian commonwealth and between the different classes in each community, any fiscal policy is certain to fail. Enjoying such sympathy and co-operation^I believe that under almost any fiscal policy Canada is certain to succeed.
"What is wrong with Canada?" Answering this question I would say a lack of teamwork; an attitude of pulling apart rather

than one of pulling together: a lack of sympathy and understanding between rural and urban interests within the community, and a prevalence of sectional interests within Canada 'herself. What is the remedy for this condition? Some few years ago when the thought laid hold of the people of Canada that the Canadian National railways were our railways, that we the people of Canada were vitally interested in their success or failure, things began to happen to the Canadian National Railway-it gained the greatest asset instrumental to the success of any organization, the good will of the people. So with the industrial and commercial life of this country. Let the people feel that Canadian industries are our industries, that Canadian farms are our farms, that the interests of both are immutably joined together, that one cannot succeed if the other fail, and that both are worth saving. When the people of Canada are actuated by such a feeling, Canada as a whole will move forward. In this connection the Farmers Advocate of April 16, last, under the editorial "The same road and the same gait" has this to say:
Capitalists, manufacturers, tradesmen, labour and urban people generally were never more convinced than now that poverty and prosperity are closely associated with the economic status and well being of the farmer. It has taken more than words and oratory to make the lesson understood. Only decreased sales, lack of employment and	a general	slowing down	of businesscould persuade	the other	classes of people that	whether they like it or not they will have to keep step with the fanner.What is throttling the life of some of our Canadian industries to-day? Lack of sales. With increased sales follows increased production. lower	overhead	costs and,	with	efficient management, more profitable returns. Develop in	Canada	the morale	that	will
boost the purchase of Canadian products. That does not mean to apply only in a limited sense to made-in-Canada boots and shoes, hats and caps and farm implements, but just as truly to Canadian eggs and cheese, butter and bacon, apples and fish. Let Canada do her best along these lines, and such a revival in trade will result as will make every legitimate industry in Canada as busy as a Canadian beaver.
The heart of the Canadian people is sound. What stands in the way of this much-to-be-desired condition? A cloud of misunderstanding seems to exist in the minds of some people that, given the privilege to enforce a system of still higher taxation upon the consumers of this country that industry and Canada as a whole will prosper. Such a system will always be resented by the people taxed. Such a system will always prove a barrier to

The Budget-Mr. Brethen
that bond of sympathy and co-operation that would ensure maximum sales within the country. When you tax the over-burdened taxpayer of East Peterborough on the implements he uses and the clothes he wears, to give the benefit of such tax to some gentleman in Toronto or Montreal, you do not add to the taxable wealth of Canada. You do hamper and prevent the just and equitable distribution of such wealth.
The United States of America has often been referred to in this debate because of the success it has attained, supposedly to the policy of protection. Mr. Coolidge, making his maiden speech in Washington on December 6, 1923, has this to say regarding United States agriculture, then and still in a deplorable state of distress:
No complicated scheme of relief, no plan for government fixing of prices, no resort to the public treasury will be of any permanent value in establishing agriculture. Simple and direct methods put in operation by the farmer himself are the only real sources for restoration.
If such words were true of agriculture in 1923, have they not been proven equally true to-day? The American farmer was hoodwinked, or hoodwinked himself, into believing that high protective tariffs would alleviate his conditions. Apparently the very reverse lias been true, and he is compelled, as have farmers in Canada, to fall back on simple and direct methods of organization and cooperative marketing.
But if the statement of President Coolidge is correct concerning agriculture, is it not equally true of industry? In Canada we have the spectacle of some industrial concerns, notably the binder twine industry of Brantford, working under simple and direct methods, put in operation by the industry itself, and buying their raw materials in the open markets of the world, working overtime, expanding its operations to the point where it is acknowledged to be the greatest of its kind in the British Empire, and paying regular dividends to its shareholders. Side by side with this industry in the city of Brantford, we have other industries enjoying special privilege in the sale of their products and given prac-ticaly free trade in the purchase of their raw material. Yet according to my hon. friends to my right, these industries are closed or in a ver}' unhealthy condition.
What conclusions can we draw from such a situation?
1.	That altogether too much emphasis has been placed upon the effect of the changes made in our tariff during the past two or three years. These changes averaging between one and two per cent are so insignificant that
they could not possibly be responsible for either the good effects claimed by the government or the bad effects claimed just as vigorously by the opposition.
2.	That the real cause-and admitted so by the representatives of industry themselves -is lack of sales.
I remember during the past year that in our caucus room we met representatives of the implement manufacturers of Brantford and they proceeded to place the industrial situation in Brantford before us. They made the statement that many factories were closed, and I asked one of the gentlemen, the spokesman of the party, "Are all the factories in Brantford in that condition?" And he said, "No, there is the binder twine industry, for instance, that is working night and day." But, he said, "Of course they have a good sale for their product." I said, "Is the question, then not one of lack of sales in all these industries?" And he admitted that if was. "Well then would the proposed increase in the protective tariff alleviate or would it aggravate that situation? Would charging a higher price enable them to sell more, to increase their sales, or would it not?" There was no answer to that question.
Now just on the side, in leaving that meeting I was informed by a gentleman from the city of Brantford that the spokesman of that party started in some years ago-and he was still a man in his prime-with praloticaMy nothing and had recently sold out one-half interest in his business for half a million dollars. He claimed that he got very little assistance from the protective tariff, that he did not use the tariff to fix his price? in any way, and yet he had made good in bis particular industry in Brantford.
Developing this conclusion that the problem is one of lack of sales I will go further and state that I do not believe the increased tariff imposed by the United States against, Canada and the world helped very materially in bringing about conditions in that country, as they exist to-day. I admit it hurt us by dislocating our trade, but it certainly did not benefit the American farmers, and I repeat that I seriously question if industry in the United States reaped any material gain. We are accustomed to this argument advanced by some hon. members; "The United States has a high protective tariff; the United States is prosperous; therefore high protective tariffs briug prosperity". But here I would like to remind my hon. friends that during r.he past winter in the highly industrialized city of Detroit the Ford motor plant, one of the most highly financed, highly organized and efficiently
The Budget-Mr. Brethen

managed industrial concerns in the world, was running but three days a week, and thousands of unemployed were almost on the bread line.
Conditions in the United States have, by way of comparison with those in Canada, entered so frequently into the discussions in this House that I will be pardoned if I refer to them. From first hand information received through personal interviews with people across the line, real estate dealers, bankers, contractors, workers in motor plants and allied industries, I have drawn the conclusion that the happy conditions in the United States we so often hear about from our friends to the right are due, not to highly protective tariff, but to the following reasons:
1.	To the tremendous financial advantage gained by the United States by her late entry into the world war.
2.	To a commendable reduction of some
85,000,000,000 in taxation during the past four years.
3.	To an immense building boom-suspended during the war period-of some $5,000,000,000 or $6,000,000,000 spread over the cities of the central and northern states.
4.	To a system of financing, the very reverse of that practised in Canada, whereby credit instead of cash sales are encouraged. Fully 90 per cent, I believe, of the sales in real estate and business contracts, in fact, almost every commercial transaction is performed on the basis of a cash payment down of 10, 15 or 20 per cent, with the balance on paper.
5.	To the fact that apparently everybody in the big cities, the real estate dealer, banker, doctor, lawyer, worker in the factory, even the nurse in the hospital, subscribes to this financial practice.
At six o'clock the House adjourned, without question being put, pursuant to rule.
